summary: Read all 13 biome definitions (record 3), the 4,300-cell biome array (16), the 15 features (12), all 157 rivers (32), all 139 icebergs (39), the grid height/precipitation/temperature arrays (7, 8, 11), record 1 geography and climate, and all 6,887 relief icons (49), and checked every burg's cell (biome, height, river, coast, lake, island) against its gazetteer entry and every annals event placed on a burg or marker. AGREE: river names and courses in the history (every one of about 45 'on the Abhainn X' claims in the gazetteer and annals matches the map, including the longest river, Abhainn ìseal); the central mountains (peak about 3,570 ft at Muileann gheal, Dùn ìseal about 2,570 ft) and the hills east of the capital; Loch chrom as the only lake; the named isles (Eilean ghorm, dhubh, mhin, dhearg, ruadh, fhada, chrom, ìseal); the dry north and east and wet west/south of the precipitation layer; relief hills/woods/bogs read as moor with valley groves. CONFLICTS fixed: (1) 616 Glacier cells under 109 farmed towns: 579 relabelled Tundra (moor), 37 inland cells of the far north-west kept as the ice cap of the frozen coast, temperatures under relabelled cells raised to -5°C, population on the frozen coast and shire 120's ice-edge cut from about 1.22 million to 21 thousand, farm goods removed there, 60 icons on the ice removed, 19 acacia icons redrawn as broad-leaved wood; (2) the capital and its 'harbours' (Cathair dhomhain, Ros dhomhain, Seann Vell, Doire fhiadhaich, Baile ghlas, Seann Warr, Doire fhada, Ceann gheal) stand on fresh Loch chrom, ten cells from the sea: history wording changed from 'coast/sea' to lake shore in 12 annals, 4 book passages, 1 appendix and 4 gazetteer entries, with the Abhainn gheal as the ships' way up from the sea (new event IV-0012a); Seann Warr's salt and salt marsh explained by brine springs; (3) terrain wording: Àth fhiadhaich and Dùn thais are hill towns not coast towns, Baile thais is above the gulf with Cidhe Beag below it, the Reòta road-house is on low moor not a high pass, Cathair mhòr is below the hills, five 'hill/upland' claims on flat ground, the west's 'dry heath' made wet heath, Cnoc fhionn's orchards and cider on the cold north-eastern moor made barley and ale, the Inis mhòr freeze made an early freeze; (4) seven 'island' towns on the main island made tidal islets or river islands; two 'river' claims with no mapped river made streams; (5) record 1 latitude 5.9-65.3 N replaced by 62.5-64.5 N to fit the 0.2-mile scale. MISSING, now written: the ice of the north (139 icebergs: drift ice, two new events I-0008a and IV-0127a; the ice cap I-0006a), the northern cooling behind the moor-and-grove north (I-0220a), the ocean's name An Cuan Siar, the unnamed isles (Eilean bhàn, gheal, bheag, dhìreach) and island towns (5 gazetteer notes), the chief rivers' sources, courses and lengths, the lake's feeders and outflow, regions and their cover, and the climate: all in the new Appendix I (appendices/I_land.md). Lengths and areas use 0.2 miles to the map unit; heights use the map's own feet.

map_edits.why: 616 land cells were labelled Glacier though 109 towns stand on them, and the history (gazetteer and annals for Doire ghlas, Baile Mòr mhòr, Tobar ghorm, Caol mhòr, Cathair naomh and the rest) describes them as moor, sheepwalk, peat, groves, farms and harbours, which the relief icons (bog and wood) and cell goods (grain, hemp, honey, wood) also show. Only the far north-western horn is ice in the history (an Oirthir Reòthte, 'under ice and tundra'). Tundra is read in the appendix as open moor.

map_edits.summary: 414 grid cells under the relabelled cells are raised to -5°C (23°F) where they were colder, so that the stored temperature agrees with the Tundra label by the generator's own rule (Glacier only below -5°C). Every other value is unchanged.
map_edits.why: Keeps temperature and biome consistent; the north stays cold (annual mean about 23°F, snowbound winters), as the appendix and Appendix G describe.

event.title: The ice keeps the north-west
event.body: When the oak comes to the lowlands the ice of the cold years draws back from all the island but its north-western horn. There a low cap of ice holds behind the shore, and it holds there still. No hearth of any age has been found under it or on it.

event.title: Seals on the drift ice
event.body: Hunters of the north shore go out on the drift ice that the northern sea brings down in late winter and take seals on it. The seal bones in the middens of the north coast carry the same cut-marks as those of Eilean mhin. The tellings of Eilean fhada count a hard year by how near the ice came.

event.title: The moor takes the north
event.body: The pollen in the bog under Doire ghlas shows the oak falling back. Heather, birch and bog-moss spread over the northern lowlands, and the groves that give the north its many Doire names shrink to the sheltered valleys, where they still stand. The tellings of the north remember it as the time the winters lengthened.

event.title: The first hull on Loch chrom
event.body: Pilots of Caol leathan bring the first of the strangers' ships up the Abhainn gheal into Loch chrom, towing her through the shallows below Baile ghlas with boats. She anchors off Ros dhomhain. From then on the humans' goods come to the capital shore by water, and the pilots charge a stranger's hull twice the toll of a Ròdaich boat.

event.title: A brig in the drift ice
event.body: A Company brig bound for the northern landing with tools is caught in the drift ice off Eilean fhada in a late spring and crushed. Her crew walk over the ice to the harbour at Caol bheag. After it the Company's charts mark the northern passage closed from midwinter to the end of spring.

text_edit.why: The frozen coast's population is lowered on the map from 397,430 to about 7,260 (record 21): sealers and fowlers on 190 square miles of frozen shore and ice.

unsure: The relief icons (3,254 broad-leaved, 2,147 grass, 1,379 bog, only 22 conifer) and the cell goods (wood, hemp, honey, wine on cold cells) look drawn from an earlier, warmer biome layer. I tested restoring that layer from the icons: goods-to-biome mismatches fall from 233 to 52 of 373. I kept the cold map instead because Appendices G and H and the economy/shire proposals already describe a cold island, and the history's snow, peat, moor and frozen coast fit it. If the owner prefers a temperate Rodos, the biome and temperature layers (records 16, 11) are what would change, and G, H and this appendix would need rewording.

Seann Warr (burg 64) was moved onto the shore of fresh Loch chrom by the earlier burg_moves pass, but the history makes it a salt port with a salt marsh (I-0016, I-0087, IV-0019, IV-0105). I explained the salt with brine springs rather than moving the town. The economy proposal also gives it the island's only olive-yard; its cell averages about 45°F, too cold for olives.

The distance-scale change to 0.2 miles per unit (markers_routes proposal and the coordinator's decision) is assumed, not proposed again here. My record 1 geography edit (mapSize, latitude, coordinates) only makes sense with it.
Appendix H's shire table and totals for shire 120 (Seann Vell) and the unshired coast need recounting after the record 21 population change. I edited only the Moot's-tally sentence.
The lake's stored surface level (feature 9, height 23.9, about 114 ft) is above the lake-shore town cells (about 50 ft). This looks like a generator quirk, so the appendix gives no lake-level height.
Marker 40, Imrich nam Pantar (the great cats' crossing of the mountains, 'the high passes'), sits on low ground on the south-west coast. It belongs to the markers layer and I have not moved it.
About 20 Àth (ford) towns and 10 Muileann (mill) towns have no mapped river within a cell. I read these as streams too small for the charts and changed only the two gazetteer lines that say 'river'.
Two 'Slaves' goods on frozen-coast cells are removed with the other farm goods. The economy layer may want to review 'Slaves' elsewhere.
